title: The empathy edge in business success
text:
The empathy edge in business success
In the competitive tech industry, confrontation is sometimes seen as spurring competitiveness. But experts – and employees – point to the value of leading with respect, humility, and curiosity in the workplace.
The creativity and competitiveness of the American tech industry are indisputable. In just a few decades, Silicon Valley-aligned firms and their founders have upended global business, demonstrating unimagined possibilities for innovation and investment. (Witness Anthropic’s $1.76 trillion debut on Wall Street Thursday.)
In the process, many tech behemoths have also toppled more traditional business-school management models, with some “move fast” CEOs perhaps viewing those approaches as relics of the pre-internet era. The pros and cons of “founder mode” or “manager mode” in running startups and established high-tech firms have been hotly debated in recent years. Founder mode makes allowances for unconventional CEO styles and behaviors that supporters see as mere personal quirks or even uniquely essential traits. But critics say this creates a false binary, which can diminish workplace respect, collaboration, and dignity, ultimately harming company cohesion and the bottom line.
This issue has come to the fore with force over the past week, with emerging media reports about the often abrasive management style of Jensen Huang, the founding CEO of tech giant Nvidia. Mr. Huang, who resigned Nov. 12, is not alone among Silicon Valley peers in eliciting both criticism and praise for the manner in which they have led their firms to success.
But even as stock valuations and profits rise, there is an apparent reconsideration taking place among a growing share of managers, employees, and the public: that values such as collegial respect and dignity, alongside empathy and humility, are both timeless and timely.
Based on interviews with 2,361 business leaders and employees in six countries including the United States, a 2025 Harvard Business Impact report listed seven “leadership superpowers”: integrity, self-awareness, empathy, courage, determination, optimism, and curiosity. The multiyear research determined that these traits “enable leaders to create positive change for their people, their organizations, and society at large.” While 77% of senior leaders saw empathy as important, only 47% said their organizations valued it.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, a consummate tech-industry insider, appears to align with such views.
“Innovation is about meeting unmet, unarticulated needs. ... Design thinking is empathy,” he told Stanford Graduate School of Business’ website Insights some years ago. His management approach, he said, emphasizes respect and empathy as a means of promoting a “culture that reflect[s] a learning organization.”
“For years, organizations have often rewarded visibility, confidence, and ambition in leaders,” according to the recruitment screening firm Hogan. But such behaviors, it noted when presenting recent research on its website in April, do not necessarily “build trust, strengthen teams, or support sustained performance.” Firms might need to “look beyond visibility or charisma,” Hogan suggested.
The list of relatively modest, even humble, “superpowers” that the Harvard report identified could serve as useful guideposts in making such a corporate shift.
